title: London AI concentration could stunt UK growth
raw_text:
About 100,000 vacancies for artificial intelligence (AI) roles were posted across the UK in the past six months, up 51% from the previous period, according to an Accenture survey.

Accenture’s Tech Talent Tracker revealed that demand for AI skills increased the overall tech jobs market by 21%. But these roles are concentrated in London, which had six times as many AI-related job listings as Manchester, Leeds, Newcastle and Liverpool combined.

In the wider tech sector, the biggest increase in demand for tech skills was in Manchester (35%), reaching more than 30,000 roles, followed by Bristol (25%) and Birmingham (17%).

London, in comparison, saw in excess of 250,000 tech jobs listed, which was a 24% increase on the previous six-month period. About two-thirds of the UK’s tech talent works in London, which equates to roughly 1.75 million people. Manchester, Leeds, Newcastle and Liverpool collectively account for just 13%, the research found.

But the survey report warned that the concentration of skills in London could stunt UK growth in the future, particularly with the increased need for AI experts nationwide.

“London’s strength as a global technology hub is undoubtedly a success story and has helped establish the UK as a serious player in AI. But as organisations race to recruit the skills needed to realise value from AI, the concentration of AI jobs and talent in one place presents a longer-term challenge for the UK’s growth ambitions,” said Sam Holmes, talent reinvention lead at Accenture UK.

“AI is not just the preserve of technology companies based in the capital. Businesses across every sector and region of the UK will need AI skills to remain competitive and unlock new sources of productivity and growth,” added Holmes. “Creating more opportunities for people to develop these skills across the country will be essential if the UK is to realise the full potential of AI, ensuring its benefits are felt in every corner of the country.”

Developers still in demand

According to Accenture’s survey, jobs that support the take-up of AI are also seeing a bounce, with listings in engineering and DevOps up 11% to 100,000, data analytics jobs up 19% to about 90,000, and cyber security roles advertised rising by almost 20%.

“The findings indicate that AI is reshaping technology roles rather than reducing demand for them. As businesses move from AI experimentation to embedding it meaningfully into their operations, a combination of engineers and data expertise is becoming increasingly important in building and integrating the systems that underpin it,” said Accenture.

Organisations may also look to reskill experienced tech professionals to enable them to combine their know-how with AI skills, because a large portion of the AI skills base is people in the early stages of their careers. The survey found that 40% of professionals with AI skills have fewer than six years’ professional experience, with about a quarter with two years’ experience or less.

“The findings suggest organisations may increasingly look to build AI capabilities through training and reskilling from a broader base of technical expertise, alongside specialist hiring,” said Accenture.

Holmes echoed a claim made by Infosys chairman Nandan Nilekani at the recent Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, where he described fears that AI would take tech jobs as “hogwash”.

Holmes said: “As organisations become more mature in how they use AI, demand is growing for the engineers, developers and data specialists needed to deploy and scale it effectively.”

He added: “Far from reducing the need for talent, AI is increasing demand for a wider mix of technology skills. Competition for AI expertise is already intensifying, meaning organisations will need to invest in developing talent alongside recruiting it if they are to keep pace with demand.”

But Sam Kingston, CEO of software services company Zenitech and former UK head of EDS’s UK private sector business, said the argument “won’t hold”.

“I agree to a point, but then it will drop, and it won’t create jobs,” he said. “It will actually make people more efficient, and that then means that the speed of delivery is faster, and you’ll also use fewer people, senior and qualified people, to do that.”

Kingston said mid-level and junior-level workers will be hit in the beginning, as those in senior roles will be working alongside AI.

title: MoD’s new SIEM, analytics platform up and running
raw_text:
The UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) has successfully deployed an upgraded security information and event management (SIEM) and analytics platform for its Defence Cyber Operations (DCO) team.

The new service is being delivered by IT services house Centerprise, which is overseeing commercial delivery, support, enablement and governance, and Elastic, which will take on the core SIEM capabilities – with the intent of ensuring the MoD’s cyber operators can get up and running quickly and without fuss.

“DCO deserves a platform that can grow with the scale of the challenge. Together with Elastic, we are building that capability while ensuring the MoD has the support to use it effectively from day one,” said Centerprise director of defence and security, Mark Brady.

“Our structured governance and enablement approach ensures the MoD achieves maximum value and long-term resilience from this platform.”

Faith Bateman, regional vice president of public sector at Elastic, added: “The MoD’s continued investment in cyber defence reflects its commitment to staying ahead of an increasingly complex hybrid threat environment, where adversaries operate across cyber, information and physical domains simultaneously.

“Through our work with DCO and Centerprise, we are enabling analysts to maintain a common operational picture across the entire environment, centralising data to accelerate detection and mission response, and allowing analysts to focus on high-priority threats,” said Bateman.

Traditional SIEM not up to the job

The core challenge facing the MoD’s new partners arose from the fact that its globally-distributed military and ancillary workforce demands its networks must not only be constantly available but able to handle large volumes of extremely sensitive traffic, often relating to intelligence or military operations

The MoD had found that more traditional SIEM platforms were unable to keep pace with the ever more sophisticated cyber threats faced by a department of its nature. Historically, this led to visibility gaps and rendered its incident responders slower and less effective. Lacking strong governance and enablement meant even more advanced tools could never live up to their potential.

According to Centerprise and Elastic, the new, refined programme equips DCO with a “defence-ready” SIEM capability that will deliver more unified visibility, streamlined operations, and faster incident detection and response.

Some of the system’s public features include expanded visibility across the MoD’s networks to let cyber operators spot and contain malicious activity before it becomes a problem, and easier to follow workflows to ensure cyber responders can work quicker and ensure incidents don’t disrupt core military missions.

Meanwhile, structured training and oversight will hopefully help the MoD ensure its new platform is able to adapt as the threat landscape continues to evolve

The system’s resilience is underpinned by a tiered support model via which Elastic will take responsibility for providing advanced technical expertise, while Centerprise looks after orchestration, escalation and governance.

Hybrid warfare

The MoD’s latest deployment comes amid a growing threat from hybrid cyber-kinetic military operations targeting European states, which some authorities believe is in danger of spilling over into open war, likely against Russia.

In such a scenario, the true threat to the UK’s security would likely come not as it did during the Second World War – from a Nazi ground invasion – but from the kind of tactics used in Ukraine, such as electronic warfare and cyber attacks on digital infrastructure and communications networks, food suppliers, government bodies and utilities.

In his annual speech assessing the threats facing the UK, delivered earlier this week, MI5 chief Ken McCallum spoke of a “generational shift” in national security and spoke of how artificial intelligence (AI) in particular is “supercharging the cyber security contest”.

title: UK data watchdog warns Met Police over shadow IT data breach
raw_text:
The Metropolitan Police Service has been reprimanded after police officers and staff uploaded sensitive personal data about suspects to an unapproved web platform used by retailers to track shoplifters.

The Information Commission’s Office warned that the incident reflected an “ongoing failure” by the police service to install technical restrictions to prevent staff using unauthorised services, or shadow IT, for police work.

The ICO found that measures put in place by the Metropolitan Police to prevent staff using an unauthorised facial recognition application Clearview, four years earlier had failed to prevent a similar incident occurring.

The data protection watchdog said in a reprimand issued on 15 October that police officers and staff had put individuals at risk by posting details about people suspected of shoplifting on a web platform used by retailers to deter shoplifting.

The Auror platform, which is owned by a New Zealand-based company, allows retailers to record and analyse shoplifting incidents using facial recognition, automatic number plate recognition and artificial intelligence.

Retailers can upload incident reports, images and CCTV footage which they can share with police officers. Police officers, who are given free accounts on the platform, can also share information with retailers about suspects.

Police use of Auror was ‘high risk’

An investigation by the ICO found that the platform, which is used by retailers including Tesco, Boots, M&S, Greggs, Holland and Barrett and Home Bargains, was being used by MPS officers and staff without the knowledge of the police force and without having adequate security in place to protect sensitive data.

The MPS claims to have alerted the ICO as soon as it became aware of the problem in September 2024, but the ICO reported that it had only learned of the incident during a discussion about a separate matter in December 2024.

The use of an unapproved platform to identify potential criminal offenders was likely to result in a “high risk” to the people affected, including misidentification as an offender, being banned from premises, having their movements restricted or damage to their reputation, the ICO found.

According to the Metropolitan Police Service, retailers encouraged police officers to sign up to the Auror  platform to review CCTV evidence of reported crimes from early 2023.

The police officers were sent QR codes by Auror Europe, which used MPS branding on its website, to allow them to create their own free accounts on the service.

A subsequent investigation revealed that Police Officers and staff created 500 accounts, of which 375 were actively used. The MPS said it did not have information on how frequently officers had accessed the platform.

Police staff identified 179 unique individuals, of which 59 were arrested, charged or convicted or had their information circulated as a wanted person after being identified on the Auror platform.

An internal review found that police officers and staff had shared sensitive personal information, including the names of suspects, dates of birth, addresses and in some cases references to use of facial recognition software. It also included information about three people under the age of 18.

The names, warrant numbers and email addresses of MPS officers were also shared on the Auror platform.

Missed opportunities to identify problem

The ICO’s investigation revealed the police service missed multiple opportunities to restrict the use of the platform, which had been used by MPS staff since March 2023, before finally taking action

In June that year, for example, a police officer, who no longer works for the force, submitted a request to have access to a mobile version of the platform, Auror Frontline, which was approved in principle by a committee 18 days later, without raising any alerts.

In August 2024, the MPS had another opportunity to shut the system down, when a security incident report found that a member of staff had uploaded the names of suspects they recognised in CCTV images shared by a retailer to Auror.

The police force took action to restrict the platform after a second incident report a month later that found officers were using the Auror  platform to collect CCTV images from retail outlets during investigations.

Ongoing failures

The ICO said that the failings form part of a broader and ongoing failure to ensure that the processing of data by MPS officers and staff on third party systems is carried out securely.

There was an “ongoing failure” to implement further technical restrictions to prevent staff using unauthorised services.

“The MPS failed, and continues to fail, to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that the processing of personal data by its officers and staff using third party online services…is subject to appropriate levels of assessment, approval and organisational oversight,” the ICO stated.

The ICO also found that the MPS had failed to demonstrate that it had taken appropriate steps to ensure all officers and staff had read and understood its data protection policies and had received regular training.

Met Police now using Auror

The MPS signed a formal contract with Auror Europe in December 2025 and began using the system operationally to fight shoplifting in January this year.

Police officers are now restricted from uploading and sharing data on the platform and must access the platform through a secure authentication system.

The MPS announced in August 2026 that it had completed a pilot of Auror in six London boroughs and would roll it out in another eight boroughs, after seeing improvements in the clear-up rate for shoplifting offences.

“Following formal approval and a pilot, the platform is now used in 14 London boroughs. It helps officers identify shoplifters more quickly, enabling retailers to directly share evidence and CCTV at the point of reporting and has quadrupled positive outcomes for shoplifting,” a spokesperson said. 

Lessons not learned from Clearview

The ICO found that many of the failings with Auror echoed those identified several years earlier in 2021, when the ICO reprimanded the MPS over staff’s use of an unauthorised facial recognition platform, Clearview AI, to investigate criminal offences.

Although the MPS had introduced a range of improvements and safeguards before reintroducing Auror in January 2026, the ICO said the police force needed to improve how it identifies and assesses third-party services used to process personal information.

“The MPS has failed to demonstrate that its current technical and organisational measures are appropriate to ensure an appropriate level of security for the personal data it processes,” the ICO stated.

David Doodson, ICO Head of Investigations, said that police forces hold large volumes of sensitive personal information and must have robust safeguards in place to protect it. 

“Before introducing new systems or platforms, they must properly assess the risks, put appropriate safeguards in place and ensure effective oversight,” he added.

An MPS spokesperson said that it accepted the ICO’s findings that data protection arrangements at the time were insufficient.

“While officers were using the platform in good faith to identify and arrest shoplifters, we recognise that we had not completed the relevant security and data protection work for the platform to be used,” the spokesperson added.

Auror timeline

3 December 2021: The ICO reprimands the MPS after two employees use the Clearview AI facial recognition platform without appropriate corporate oversight or authorisation.

March 2023: The Auror  platform, used by retailers to record and report shoplifting and anti-social behaviour, is made available to officers and staff of the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS).

9 June 2023: A police officer, who is no longer employed by the MPS, submits a request form to use the "Auror Frontline" mobile app. The MPS claims the officer wrongly tells other MPS staff that Auror has been approved for use in the police service, and awareness of the service spreads by word of mouth.

27 June 2023: The request form is considered by a Mobile Applications Approval Meeting (MAAM) without a representative of the MPS' data protection team being present. The meeting agrees to approve the use of the Auror App with caveats, including setting up a single-sign-on capability and the continued monitoring of all members of staff. The MAAM does not carry out a Data Protection Impact Assessment, on the grounds that the officer making the request has not indicated that one is necessary. Officers are unable to use the app, however, because it is blocked by IT security controls.

29 August 2024: An MPS security incident report finds that a member of staff has been using Auror and has uploaded the full names of suspects they recognise in CCTV images shared by a retailer. It finds that Auror is also used by other teams in the MPS to prepare case files.

26 September 2024: A second security incident report finds that MPS officers are using the Auror  platform to collect CCTV images from retail outlets, even though the platform has not been approved by MPS cyber security and no checks have been undertaken.

The MPS blocks access to Auror on its systems and establishes a "Gold Group" led by a senior commander to identify and mitigate the risks of using Auror.

October 2024: The MPS instructs all staff not to use the Auror platform and initiates an internal risk assessment. It asks Auror Europe to remove all MPS branding from its website.

December 2024: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) becomes aware of the MPS' use of Auror during discussions about a different matter.

17 February 2025: The MPS informs the ICO that officers have accessed and used the Auror  platform before the MPS "corporately became aware of it."

4 April 2025: A Met Police Operational Risk Board Review reports that Auror was made available to MPS officers in 2023 without having been formally adopted for use by the police force.

10 April 2025: The ICO initiates a formal investigation into the processing of personal data on the Auror  platform.

16 May 2025: The MPS informs the ICO that it first becomes aware of the use of Auror after the August security incident report is escalated to the Professional Standards Unit.

11 December 2025: The MPS signs a formal contract with Auror Europe.

26 January 2026: The MPS re-enables Auror for operational use. Police officers are now restricted from uploading and sharing data on the platform and must access the platform through a secure authentication system.

There was an “ongoing failure” to implement further technical restrictions to prevent staff using unauthorised services.

“The MPS failed, and continues to fail, to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that the processing of personal data by its officers and staff using third party online services…is subject to appropriate levels of assessment, approval and organisational oversight,” the ICO stated.

The ICO also found that the MPS had failed to demonstrate that it had taken appropriate steps to ensure all officers and staff had read and understood its data protection policies and had received regular training.

Met Police now using Auror

The MPS signed a formal contract with Auror Europe in December 2025 and began using the system operationally to fight shoplifting in January this year.

Police officers are now restricted from uploading and sharing data on the platform and must access the platform through a secure authentication system.

The MPS announced in August 2026 that it had completed a pilot of Auror in six London boroughs and would roll it out in another eight boroughs, after seeing improvements in the clear-up rate for shoplifting offences.

title: Computer Weekly announces the Most Influential Women in UK Tech 2026
raw_text:
Karen Blake, co-author of the Lovelace Report and head of EDIS, has become the 15th person to be named Computer Weekly’s most influential woman in UK technology.

The list was created in 2012 to make the amazing women in the UK’s technology sector more visible and accessible, originally showcasing only 25 women before growing to include 50 women in 2015.

Now, the list receives hundreds of nominations each year – this year’s longlist features more than 870 women.

Alongside the longlist and top 50, Computer Weekly and a collection of expert judges also choose entrants to its Hall of Fame to acknowledge those who have made a lifetime contribution to the tech sector, and a selection of Women to Watch (formerly Rising Stars) who are expected to continue to do great things over the next few years.

This year’s winner has previously been a judge for the list, before joining the top 50 in 2025, and has done invaluable work to increase representation in the technology sector.

Here is the list of the 50 Most Influential Women in UK Technology 2026.

1. Karen Blake, co-author, the Lovelace Report; head, EDIS; member, Women in Tech Taskforce

Karen Blake currently heads up Equality, Diversity and Inclusion in Science and Health (EDIS), a coalition of organisations from the science and health sectors looking to build a more inclusive research system for health in the UK.

Until September 2026, she was on the strategy steering board of Women Pivoting to Digital at the City of London Corporation and is a Women in Tech Taskforce member for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. Until it was disbanded, she was co-CEO of the Tech Talent Charter, where she led the organisation’s growth and headed up the implementation of some of the tools it offered, such as its benchmarking platform and annual benchmarking reports.

She was a co-author of the recent Lovelace Report, and until November 2025, was head of inclusive workforce strategy and advisory at Powered By Diversity. Previously, Blake was a senior researcher for the House of Commons looking into digital inclusion policies, and a freelance inclusive practice business consultant.

2. Deborah O’Neill, partner and head of technology innovation UKI and Nordics, Oliver Wyman

Deborah O’Neill was appointed head of technology innovation for the UK, Ireland and the Nordics at Oliver Wyman in early 2025. She is also head of performance transformation for the UK, Ireland and the Nordics at the firm, and before that was head of digital for Europe, where she led digital transformation and new proposition launches at companies all over the world.

Alongside this, she is also a strategic partner at FutureDotNow and a board trustee for Girlguiding. She was a co-author on the recent Lovelace Report, which detailed the reasons women are leaving the technology sector.

3. Blaise Metreweli, chief of the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6)

The only publicly named member of staff for MI6, Blaise Metreweli, referred to as “C”, heads up the organisation tasked with keeping the UK safe, and reports directly to the foreign secretary.

Metreweli joined MI6 in 1999, and has held many roles within the organisation in the past, including director general for technology and innovation, a role often referred to as “Q”.

4. Angela McLean, chief scientific adviser, UK government

Since 2023, Angela McLean has been the government’s chief scientific adviser, responsible for providing scientific advice to the prime minister.

McLean has a background in mathematical biology and zoology, and aims to use this knowledge, as well as her interest in mathematical models, to help the government understand the spread of infectious diseases.

She has been on the receiving end of many awards and accolades for her work, and in 1994, she established Mathematical Biology at the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council’s Institute for Animal Health.              

5. Mary McKenna, co-founder, AwakenHub and AwakenAngels

Mary McKenna is a huge supporter of entrepreneurship and startups, holding several roles as an adviser and investor. Her social enterprise, AwakenHub, where she is co-founder, is focused on building a community of female founders in Ireland.

As well as being an expert adviser for the European Commission, she is an entrepreneurship expert with the Entrepreneurship Centre at the University of Oxford’s Said Business School, and a board member for Coinvest Capital, among many other board memberships and non-executive directorships.

In 2013, she was awarded an MBE for services to digital technology, innovation and learning.

6. Erin Platts, CEO, Octopus Ventures; member, board of trustees, Founders Pledge

Erin Platts is currently the CEO of venture capital and private venture firm Octopus Ventures, as well as a member of the board of trustees for Founders Pledge.

In the past, she has been CEO of HSBC Innovation Banking in the UK, and a board member for UK Finance and the ScaleUp Institute. She is outspoken about the importance of diversity and inclusion in tech and finance, and is a UK trustee at Founders Pledge, an advisory board member for London Tech Week and a member of the Capital Markets Industry Taskforce.

She has been named an Innotribe Power Woman in Fintech, and was named in Management Today’s Top 35 Women under 35.

7. Zahra Shah, board adviser, NexaQuanta; chair and founding member, Women in AI Working Group, UKAI

Zahra Shah’s career is deeply focused on AI – she is currently a board adviser for responsible AI consultancy and services firm NexaQuanta, and is also a founding member and chair of the UKAI Women in AI Working Group.

She is also a co-founder, investor and non-executive director for AI privacy and consent management platform Seers, as well as a senior board adviser and investment committee member for Teamup Ventures.

Until recently, she was an adviser on artificial intelligence for the Commonwealth Businesswomen’s Network.

8. Danielle George, chief scientific adviser for national security, GCHQ; professor and vice-dean at the University of Manchester

With more than 25 years as a lecturer in radio frequency engineering at the University of Manchester, Danielle George was appointed chief scientific adviser for national security at GCHQ in 2025.

She is also the vice-president at the University of Manchester and a fellow of BCS.

In the past, George has been president of the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET), and in 2016 was appointed an OBE for services to engineering through public engagement.

9. Zoe Kleinman, technology and AI editor, BBC

Zoe Kleinman has been with the BBC since 2003, originally joining as a features editor of staff newspaper Ariel. She then became a web producer for Working Lunch on BBC Two, and was a senior technology reporter for the BBC, before becoming a radio presenter on technology and business-themed shows such as the BBC Tech Tent.

Now, she’s the technology and AI editor for BBC News, covering technology news across BBC radio, TV and digital.

10. Claire Reid, chief technology and innovation officer and head of PwC Women in Tech, PwC UK

Claire Reid has been with PwC for more than 25 years, holding several roles including regional leader for Scotland, UK forensics services leader and UK Management Board head of risk. She is currently the firm’s chief technology and innovation officer and head of PwC Women in Tech in the UK.

She’s passionate about creating inclusive environments where the right people can engage with the right technology.

11. Samantha Niblett, MP, founder, Labour Women in Tech

Before her time as an MP, Samantha Niblett had a long career in technology, holding roles such as industry sales leader at DXC Technology and head of alliances, channel and ecosystem in EMEA at 1E.

Now, alongside her role as an MP, she’s the founder of the Labour: Women in Tech group, which campaigns to reach equal gender opportunities in the technology industry.

Until recently, she was the co-chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on FinTech, chair of the Interparliamentary Forum on Emerging Technologies, and a member of the Women and Equalities Select Committee.

12. Avril Chester, co-founder, The Human Intelligence Circle; founder, Cancer Central; CEO, AINAD

Award-winning entrepreneur Avril Chester is currently chief operating officer and advisory board member at artificial intelligence (AI) venture studio AINAD.

She also co-founded the Human Intelligence Circle, a movement to encourage individuals to “lead with humanity” in the wake of AI. As part of this project, she authored a book, bringing together 30 leaders to share their perspective on how to achieve this goal.

She was previously the chief technology officer (CTO) of the Royal Pharmaceutical Society, CTO of RIBA, and has had a long-standing career in technology and project management. In 2018, she founded technology charity platform Cancer Central to help support people with cancer.

13. Amy Low, CEO, AbilityNet

Amy Low has been chief executive of AbilityNet since August 2024, a charity aimed at using technology to reduce barriers to inclusion in work, education and life. Prior to her current position, she held other roles at the charity, including service delivery director and chief operating officer.

She is also a community board member for the Digital Poverty Alliance, as well as an Inclusive Online Services subcommittee member at the Digital Inclusion Action Committee and a strategic expert partner at the digital inclusion coalition The Connection Project.

She was named a Computer Weekly Rising Star in 2025.

14. Amanda Brock, CEO, Open UK

Amanda Brock’s role at OpenUK sees her leading the sustainable and ethical development of open technologies in the UK, including technology such as open source software, hardware and data.

Recently, she was a member of the board for the UK Open Multimodal AI Network (UKOMAIN). She also sits on the boards of the Mojaloop Foundation and US cyber security firm Mimoto, as well as acting as an advisory board member for Scarf and The Stack. In summer 2025, she became an Expert Network of the Digital Innovation Board member for the International Telecommunication Union, and is an honorary professor at the University of Bristol Smart Internet Lab.

Past experience saw her as a member of the Cabinet Office Open Standards Board, and an advisory board member for Tech All Stars and FerretDB.

15. Akua Opong, senior EUC engineer, infrastructure and cloud engineering, London Stock Exchange; STEM adviser

As well as her work as senior EUC engineer, infrastructure and cloud engineering at the London Stock Exchange Group, Akua Opong is a freelancer and science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM) adviser. She wears several hats at the London Stock Exchange, including UK chapter lead for its WINTech Network and co-lead of the London Chapter for Accessibility Network.

Until last year, she was part of the City of London Corporation volunteer advisory group for equality, diversity and inclusion, and was previously an advisory board member for Neurodiversity in Business, and a mentor at the TechUp mentor programme for Durham University.

Opong was a contributor for Voices in the shadows, the book of black female role models created by the 2022 Computer Weekly most influential woman in UK tech, Flavilla Fongang.

Currently, Opong is an award judge for WeAreTheCity, a volunteer for the Festival of The Girl, and until November 2025 was a role model and mentor for the STEMazing mentorship programme. She spent two years as a non-executive director for Genius Within CIC.            

16. Roni Savage, managing director, Jomas Associates (Engineering & Environmental)

As managing director of Jomas Associates (Engineering & Environmental), Roni Savage specialises in geotechnical and environmental engineering.

She is also passionate about topics such as women in engineering and social mobility, and is on the UK government’s Business Growth Forum (formerly the SME Business Council).

17. Lila Ibrahim, chief AI readiness officer, Google DeepMind

Lila Ibrahim has been in the tech sector for more than 30 years, and recently became chief AI readiness officer for Google DeepMind. In 2018, she was named Google DeepMind’s first chief operating officer (COO), looking after teams in disciplines such as engineering, virtual environments, programme management and operations.

Prior to this role, she was COO of online skills platform Coursera, and has also acted as general manager for emerging markets platforms in China for Intel.

18. Sarah Winmill, digital functional leader, Royal Navy, Ministry of Defence; president and chair of trustees, BCS

In her role at the Ministry of Defence, Sarah Winmill is the digital functional leader for the Royal Navy, and has previously been the MoD’s head of software products and chief information officer of business functions. She is also president and chair of trustees for the BCS.

Before her current role, Winmill was with the British Transport Police between 2016 and 2019, originally as acting CTO and then acting CIO.

She has a history of working with not-for-profit organisations, having been head of IT at the Royal Academy of Arts, head of information systems services at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and chair of Charity IT Leaders.                   

19. Jade Leung, vice-chair, AI Security Institute; security adviser to government AI taskforce

As well as being vice-chair of the UK’s AI Security Institute, Jade Leung is a distinguished visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University.

Until recently, she was the UK AI Security Institute’s CTO for AI, and the prime minister’s AI adviser, responsible for working alongside the prime minister on the use of emerging AI technologies to achieve the UK government’s Plan for Change.

In the past, she was governance lead of OpenAI and head of research and partnerships for the Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI).

20. Sarah Underhill, HR director, technology and data (Group Chief Operating Office), Lloyds Banking Group

Sarah Underhill has spent her entire career at Lloyds Banking Group, since joining the firm as a graduate in 1999. She has held several roles at Lloyds, and is currently HR director for technology and data, part of the firm’s Group Chief Operating Office, where she is responsible for developing its people strategies for technology.

She previously sat on the board of the now-disbanded tech diversity collective, Tech Talent Charter. She was named a Computer Weekly Rising Star in 2024.

21. Tessa Clarke, co-founder and CEO, Olio

Tessa Clarke co-founded and is CEO of food-sharing app Olio, which helps users share food that would otherwise be wasted.

She is a fellow of business fund Unreasonable, an advisory board member for Stop Ecocide International and, until recently, was a venture partner for early-stage generalist impact fund Mustard Seed Maze.

She has previously been a business mentor for Virgin StartUp, and works alongside the minister for small business and the Department for Business and Trade, advising on SMEs.

22. Claire Thorne, adviser and venture partner, Deep Science Ventures; council member, The Foundation for Science and Technology

Claire Thorne is currently a venture partner at Deep Science Ventures, as well as a council member at The Foundation for Science and Technology, an advisory board member for SXSW Pitch 2027 board, and an industry advisory board member for TechSkills (part of TechUK).

Until recently, Thorne was co-CEO of Tech She Can, a charity aimed at increasing the number of women in the technology sector.

She has a background in the education sector, previously holding roles as director of innovation strategy for the University of Surrey and executive officer to the vice-president (innovation) at Imperial College London.

She has also been a diversity and inclusion advisory board member for the Institute of Coding, and sat on the principal partner board at Tech Talent Charter.

23. Joanna Cavan, managing director, UK Telecoms Lab

As managing director of the UK Telecoms Lab, Joanna Cavan is responsible for the organisation’s strategy, performance and growth as it tests and researches the security and resilience of UK telecoms.

Until recently, she was a board member for research network GRIIT (Gender Equity Research and Inclusive Innovation in Technology) and a board member of the West Midlands Defence and Security Cluster.

Cavan has a long-standing background in the public sector, having previously worked for West Mercia Police, the UK Home Office and GCHQ.

24. Caroline O’Brien, CEO, Compound Semiconductor Applications (CSA) Catapult

With a background in semiconductors, Caroline O’Brien currently heads up the Compound Semiconductor Applications (CSA) Catapult.

Previous roles have seen her as CEO of Kubos Semiconductors, general manager of Ultrahaptics and managing director of Tectonic Elements Ltd.     

25. Sam Kini, chief digital and technology officer, Unilever

Sam Kini is the chief digital and technology officer at Unilever, before which she had a dual role as global chief information officer (CIO) and chief information security officer (CISO) at the firm.

She is also a non-executive director at Verisure and was previously a sponsor and digital board adviser for a LEAD Network Digital Chapter focused on empowering women to grow their careers, and a non-executive director and member of the audit committee at Tele2.

She has previously been a CIO at easyJet and Telenet, and was the director of development and delivery – technology and transformation at Virgin Media.

26. Beverly Clarke, founder and CEO, Technology Books for Children; member and adviser, Digital, AI and Technology Task and Finish Group, Department for Education

Beverly Clarke is a technology expert who consults on technology education. She is the founder and CEO of Technology Books for Children, which aims to encourage children to read about technology topics.

She is currently advising the Department for Education’s Digital, AI and Technology Task and Finish Group on how the education system can be adapted to better provide digital skills to children.

She has previously been a professional development leader for the National Centre for Computing Education, and a national community manager for the BCS. She received an MBE for her work in 2024.

27. Zahra Bahrololoumi, CEO UK and Ireland, Salesforce

As CEO of Salesforce in the UK and Ireland, Zahra Bahrololoumi is responsible for the workforce in these regions across all industries and functions, and is particularly focused on ensuring its customers are ready for digital transformation.

She sits on several boards, including Business in the Community, Movement to Work and Cancer Research UK Corporate Partnerships, and is an independent non-executive director on the TSB board.

In 2023, she was awarded a CBE for services to the information technology sector.

28. Helen Wylie, director general, digital and transformation group, Department for Work and Pensions

Helen Wylie has been with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) for the past eight years, originally as digital delivery director before becoming CTO, then CDIO, and she is now director general of the digital and transformation group.

Prior to joining DWP, she had been head of technology delivery at the Bank of England, software development director at Experian and technology manager at Experian Payments.

29. Francesca Carlesi, CEO, Revolut UK

Francesca Carlesi’s background is in finance, having spent 15 years in the industry. She is currently CEO of fintech firm Revolut, where she’s been since 2023.

In addition to acting as a non-executive director for UK Finance, she volunteers as a young global leader for the World Economic Forum, and is a member of the Italian members organisation Valore D. She was previously co-founder and CEO of digital mortgage lending platform Molo Finance, and has worked at other large financial firms and banks, such as Barclays and Deutsche Bank.

She has been nominated for Computer Weekly’s Most Influential Women in UK Tech several times, appearing on the longlist in previous years.

30. Janine Hirt, CEO, Innovate Finance

Janine Hirt joined Innovate Finance in 2015 as the industry body’s head of community, before eventually becoming its CEO six years later. She now heads up the organisation, aiming to drive innovation and transformation in the fintech sector to make it more inclusive.

She has worked around the world in a variety of roles, including acting head of corporate relations for Chatham House in the UK, head of membership for the Brazilian-American Chamber of Commerce in New York, and head new hire trainer for an English language training programme in Japan.

31. Laura Gilbert, senior director of AI, Tony Blair Institute

Laura Gilbert is the senior director of AI at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, as well as a visiting professor in practice for the London School of Economics and Political Science.

Until recently, she was head of AI for government at the Ellison Institute of Technology Oxford, and director of the Incubator for AI at 10 Downing Street.

32. Nikita Thakrar, co-founder and CEO, Included VC

Nikita Thakrar founded and is CEO of Included VC, a venture capital fund dedicated to making sure diverse entrepreneurs gain the funding they need.

It’s not her first time working with entrepreneurs – previously she headed up innovation and entrepreneurship in Deep Science Ventures at Imperial College London.

She was named a Computer Weekly Rising Star in 2024.

33. Sharron Gunn, group CEO, BCS – The Chartered Institute for IT

In her role as group CEO for BCS – The Chartered Institute for IT, Sharron Gunn is responsible for overseeing the organisation’s drive to ensure technology has a positive impact on society.

In 2019, she was awarded an International Alliance for Women World of Difference Award.

34. Tristi Tanaka, member, BCS Community Support Committee

Tristi Tanaka is currently a member of the BCS Community Support Committee and, until recently, was chair of BCS Women and is on the community support committee for BCS, and head of the CMO Office for NHS Black Country ICB.

Previously, she was a fellow, independent audit of AI systems, for ForHumanity, part of the programme team for All4Health&Care, a community launched during the pandemic to connect digital healthcare providers with the public sector, and BCS Women membership secretary.

35. Irene Graham, CEO, Scaleup Institute

Alongside many non-executive and advisory roles, Irene Graham is currently CEO of not-for-profit organisation the Scaleup Institute.

She is also a visiting professor of entrepreneurship at Strathclyde University, as well as a board member for Creative UK.

Previously, she worked as managing director of the British Bankers Association and managing director of Standard Chartered Bank.

36. Alex Depledge, founder and executive director, Resi; entrepreneurship adviser to the chancellor of the exchequer

Alex Depledge is a serial entrepreneur who founded domestic cleaning marketplace Hassle.com and residential architecture firm Resi, where she was CEO for almost 10 years before becoming executive director in 2025. She has previously been a board member for the London Economic Action Partnership (Leap) and a non-executive director for retail analytics firm Edited.

Until March 2016, Depledge was a board member for lobbying body The Sharing Economy, and until January 2017, acted as the venture partner for startup capital firm Ignite 100. Depledge was also previously the chair of not-for-profit The Coalition for a Digital Economy (Coadec) and started her tech career as a management consultant for Accenture.

Currently, Depledge is an entrepreneurship adviser to the chancellor of the exchequer at HM Treasury.

37. Katie Gallagher, managing director, Manchester Digital; chair, UK Tech Cluster Group

Katie Gallagher heads up Manchester Digital, and also co-founded the Cyber Resilience Centre for Greater Manchester, both of which support businesses in the Manchester area.

Alongside this, she is chair of the UK Tech Cluster Group, which regularly discusses the technology issues affecting particular areas in the UK.

38. Sarah Thomson, head of tech UK, Postcode Lottery

In her decade-long career at the Postcode Lottery, Sarah Thomson has held many roles, including service and release manager, process manager and head of IT for data services.

Now, she heads up the organisation’s tech in the UK, and is a frequent speaker at women in tech events.

39. Elizabeth Anderson, CEO, Digital Poverty Alliance

In her role as CEO of the Digital Poverty Alliance, Elizabeth Anderson manages the not-for-profit’s programmes, operations and stakeholders involved in its goal to end digital poverty by 2030.

She has had a long career in the charity and not-for-profit sector, having been CEO of the British Interplanetary Society and government liaison officer for the UK Youth Climate Coalition, as well as strategic projects lead and Kensington Academy director at The Aldridge Foundation and corporate affairs business manager at Openreach.   

40. Debbie Weinstein, president, Google EMEA

Currently the president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), Debbie Weinstein has been at Google for almost 13 years, holding various roles such as vice-president of global advertising solutions, Google and YouTube, and vice-president and managing director in the UK and Ireland.

Prior to her current role, she was vice-president of global media at Unilever, and vice-president of advertising sales at Viacom, now called Paramount.

41. Jemma Davis, founder and managing director, Culture Gem; founder, DECID:R

With a long-standing career in cyber, Jemma Davis founded Culture Gem in 2017 with a focus on security culture, cyber resilience and crisis preparedness. She is currently the managing director.

She also founded DECID:R, a simulation platform that allows specialists such as incident managers, business continuity managers or crisis teams to test the outcome of their decisions should an incident occur.

Currently, Davis is head of community engagement for the WiTCH – Women in Tech and Cyber Hub, a cyber transformation consultant for Holland and Barrett. Previously, she has held cyber and consultancy-based roles in organisations such as the UK Health Security Agency, NHS Test and Trace, and Photobox.

42. Casey Calista, director and advisory board chair, Labour Digital

The chair of Labour Digital, Casey Calista has a history in both technology and the public sector. Alongside her role at Labour Digital, she is responsible for UK youth and AI governance public policy at Meta, and co-founded the network Women in Tech Policy.

She previously headed up policy and public affairs at UK scaleup Vorboss, and founded the UK public affairs tech practice at Hill+Knowlton Strategies.

She volunteers as a steering committee member for the City of London Corporation’s Women Pivoting to Digital Taskforce, and until recently was an adviser for digital citizenship charity Glitch and a policy board member for OpenUK.

43. Yvonne Gallagher, digital director, National Audit Office

With 30 years of tech and digital experience behind her, Yvonne Gallagher is currently digital director at the National Audit Office and has previously been CIO for two government departments.

She is currently a fellow at the BCS, having previously been on the organisation’s public policy and affairs board, and chair of the organisation and employer board.

Previously, she has held roles in organisations such as Network Rail, Prudential UK and Affinity Sutton.

44. Alison Kay, vice-president and managing director, AWS UK & Ireland

In her role at Amazon Web Services (AWS), Alison Kay uses her background in business model transformation to drive innovation through utilising emerging trends and technologies, while also focusing on creating an inclusive culture. She also uses her 25 years of experience in business and technology to mentor and sponsor others in the sector.

Alongside her role at AWS, Kay is a non-executive director at Lloyd’s Register, executive chairman for the Birmingham Panthers, and a board member of the UK Investment Council.

Previously, she has held roles such as senior executive at Accenture, and spent more than 18 years at EY in roles such as global sector leader for power and utilities, global vice-chair for industry, and managing partner and senior adviser for EMEIA.

45. Emily Middleton, director general, digital transformation (interim), Government Digital Service

Emily Middleton is currently the interim director general, digital transformation for the Government Digital Service, and was previously director general, digital centre design for the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology.

She is a trustee for Plan International UK, and has previously been a partner at Public Digital, as well as a Smart London project manager for the Greater London Authority.

46. Caroline Bellamy, executive director, Strider Technologies

Caroline Bellamy is currently the executive director at Strider Technologies, and is an advisory board member for the ONS data science campus.

Until recently, she was the first chief data and artificial intelligence officer for the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD), a role she held for six years.

She has had a long career in technology, holding roles such as database marketing manager at Sainsbury’s, director of insight and data at Centrica, director – data transformation, big data, analytics, information architecture, business intelligence at Vodafone, and chief data officer for Ordnance Survey.

She has been named on Truata’s list of Global Data Visionaries, as well as the Twenty in Data & Tech.

47. Phoebe Whitlock, barrister, Lamb Chambers; agile management team of the advisory board, Society for Computers and Law 

Phoebe Whitlock is first and foremost a barrister with legal firm Lamb Chambers, where she specialises in AI, intellectual property, technology and commercial law.

She has also been director of not-for-profit The Intellectual Property Awareness Network, which is focused on the importance of understanding intellectual property as part of business.

As well as being a trustee at Codebar, she is a lay-trustee of the Royal Microscopical Society and, until recently, was on the agile management team of the advisory board for the Society for Computers and Law.

48. Katie King, co-founder and CEO, Bio Orbit

Katie King co-founded Bio Orbit in 2023, a company focused on developing medicine in a microgravity factory to develop better cancer treatments, leading her to win the Innovator Award at the 2024 Everywoman in Tech awards. She is currently CEO of the company.

King is also currently a tech ambassador for Tech She Can, and has several past roles in the space and science sectors at organisations including Frontier Space Technologies and The Naked Scientists.

49. Margherita Della Valle, CEO, Vodafone

Originally from Italy, Margherita Della Valle’s career at Vodafone has spanned more than 30 years, and has included roles such as European chief financial officer (CFO), group CFO, and now group chief executive.

She has been recognised in Fortune magazine’s Most Powerful Women list, as well as in the Forbes list of the World’s 100 Most Powerful Women.

50. Susan Langley, Lord Mayor, City of London

Susan Langley is Lady Mayor of the City of London, chair of Gallagher UK, as well as senior independent director of Northern Rock Asset Management and Bradford and Bingley.

She was a founding member of the government’s Women’s Business Council and has been on the receiving end of countless awards and accolades.

In 2015, she was awarded an OBE for services to women in business.

This year marks the 15th time Computer Weekly has celebrated the Most Influential Women in UK Technology, yet women still make up only around 20% of the tech workforce.

Not only this, but for twomen who do make it into the tech sector, the environment means thousands are leaving their roles each year, some to move out of the sector altogether.

Karen Blake, head of EDIS and this year’s most influential woman in UK tech, says this is because the “programmatic solutions that we’ve worked on so far have been warm jumpers for a cold climate, and now we actually need to do something about that climate”.

Changing the chilly climate

One thing that is fuelling this problem is uneven distribution of power.

She says: “There has been movement in terms of representation, but in terms of power, that’s been rigidly set. And it’s very difficult to change who the decision-makers are.”

The lack of women in decision-making positions in tech is an ongoing concern, with the now-defunct Tech Talent Charter finding that women made up only 21% of senior UK tech leaders among its signatories in 2024, and Frank Recruitment Group finding that women only held a quarter of CIO positions in FTSE 100 companies in the same year.

For tech companies, seeking to alter this power imbalance can mean looking at policies for work allocation, looking at the progression pathways and skills development within their organisations, ensuring all employees are given the opportunity to progress, and supporting employee development – all mentioned in the Lovelace Report.

Women in particular can “stagnate” in a role. “It takes double the time for women to be promoted than men in tech,” says Blake, who encourages organisations to look at their own data to help understand what the current landscape looks like and how to shift it.

“In doing that, you move something in the culture, too,” she adds.

But these are “singular programmatic solutions”, and Blake points out that this is a systemic issue across the sector.

She explains: “It’s not misunderstood what we would need to do to make the change. Actually, what we need is commitment and consistency on those changes. I think there’s fear that change means a different power distribution, and that’s where we get into all of the traditional challenges around power and participation of who gets to lead, who gets to make those decisions.”

The real story around AI

With every technological shift, there’s the potential both to elevate people’s experience and to leave people behind.

Artificial intelligence (AI) development and adoption is moving quickly, and while many in the sector are doing their best to ensure it’s being built in a sustainable way that suits as many users as possible, Blake claims it’s as if they’re “moving through treacle”.  

She says: “We’re seeing that homogenised practice means the products, tools, services and approaches are all shaping a society that lots of us have real difficulties being able to participate in. I think more generally speaking, bigger questions are now being asked: Who are the architects of such a big societal shift?”

Blake has noticed a “narrative” surrounding AI that incorrectly suggests women “are adopting it at a slower rate”.

“That tells us nothing of the real story of what’s going on. I think it’s quite telling to see how these narratives are quickly depicted to keep a pecking order of where you should be and what your participation should look like,” she says.

In reality, Blake states, women are just using AI in a different manner than their male counterparts.

“Many women are adopting AI in a more sustainable way. They’re considering their use [of it]. They’re asking, ‘Where is it most applicable in my work? Is it safe? What’s my ethical position on this? Do I know how to apply this in a way that is consistent with my organisational position?’ I think there’s less shadow use of AI, and arguably that means a safer position for organisations.”

There are already issues with AI adoption, with unequal access to the technology widening the opportunity gap for women and lower-paid workers, and young girls are more concerned than boys about what the future looks like with AI.

This caution that women have about AI is an approach more of us should take. Blake argues that, with AI in its infancy and so many organisations adopting the technology out of perceived necessity rather than a business need, more needs to be done to ensure it’s being developed and adopted safely, sustainably and ethically, in a way that’s “meaningful and appropriate”.

With the UK said to be the quickest adopter of AI in the G7, Blake says: “I always think there is a word missing there. Adopter of what? Of productivity, of tools, of harm? What are we the quickest adopter of?

“I think that women are adopting at a speed we will be more grateful for when we look back on it. I often think of this as a time where it’s a kind of AI toddlerdom, where we’ve got all the crayons out of the box and we’re drawing on the walls. At some point we’ll get to a kind of teenage and adult [stage], and we’ll look back and wonder what on earth we were doing.”

Ensuring a diverse workforce can contribute to more sensible development and deployment of AI, but the issue is that while there are women working in AI, as is the case across the wider tech industry, they’re not in decision-making positions where they can make a real difference to how AI is shaped going forward.

Blake says: “One of the things I fear is women are finding themselves in those roles, for example AI ethics, and it’s becoming ‘office housework’, where you can be very busy doing it, but you’ve got no power to actually shape what happens with that product or service.”

This all comes back to the uneven distribution of power in the sector and why we need more diversity at the top of organisations.

“The lack of women in decision-making positions is once again blocking them from participating in meaningful decision-making when it comes to emerging technology,” says Blake.

Giving attention to broken bones

There is no quick fix for shifting towards a more diverse and equitable tech sector, but doing so could reduce mistakes with fast-paced emerging technologies and ensure wider distribution of tech that includes everyone.

The issue, though, according to Blake, is that “we haven’t fixed the bones of the system”, and the longer it takes, the more difficult it becomes.

She challenges senior leaders to spearhead this change, stating: “Your name is the one heard around dinner tables all over the place, where your employees will be telling stories about what’s happening in their days, and you’ve got the choice of whether you are the nightmares of their children or those that set their aspirations free.”

It has already taken a long time to make the smallest of progress towards a diverse and equitable tech workforce, and BCS claimed in a 2024 report that it will take another 283 years for the percentage of women working in the UK tech sector to match the 48% of women there are in the wider workforce if the pace stays the same.

But Blake has hope. “I would much rather think what’s the best that could happen looking at the sky rather than looking at the floor. This is changeable, this is movable. If we had consistency and commitment, we could change it,” she says.

title: AI will trade in finance markets instead of humans, says HSBC investment bank boss
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) agents could replace humans trading in financial markets in a few years, according to HSBC investment bank boss Michael Roberts.

The bank recently announced cuts to its human wealth managers with plans to replace them with AI – and traders could soon face the same prospect, with the combination of advances in AI, quantum computing and distributed ledger meaning see could replace humans trading in financial markets, said Roberts.

In an interview with Bloomberg TV, Roberts stressed that humans need to remain “in the loop”, adding: “I think quantum computing will be able to look at very complex types of market movements, and with the advent of AI – which will make that even quicker – you can see agents trading bonds using quantum computing. That’s the future.

“Advancements in AI, quantum computing and distributed ledger technology [mean that] the next two to four years are going to change the way we look at the pace, speed and scope of what we are trading.”

HSBC, like its competitors, is applying AI to parts of its business that might not have been seen possible a few years ago, but technology is advancing quickly in the areas of AI and quantum computing.

Earlier this month, in its announcement that it will replace human wealth managers with AI, the bank stated: “HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider. We’re continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally enabled products and journeys to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers.”

In July, the bank announced that it was launching an AI centre of excellence in Singapore, with the aim to recruit 100 AI specialists. The plan was for the centre to start applying AI to customer wealth journey conversations as one of its initial focuses.  

Banks are using AI across their businesses to reduce human intervention. In June, ING announced its pilot of an AI agent to process mortgages had been a success and that it was extending it. Today, it is live in the Netherlands. The AI agent looks over applications to understand them, explain possible outcomes and ways to move forward, and then a human employee will make final assessments and decisions.

Marco Li Mandri, change lead for scalable agentic products at ING, said there are no planned job cuts in relation to ING’s implementation of AI for mortgages, but hinted there could be in other areas. “Not for this use case,” he said. 

Another area AI can add huge commercial value is supporting investment bankers in deal making, according to Bahadir Yilmaz, chief analytics officer at ING. “Investment bankers work on deals,” said Yilmaz. “And these deals can take from six months to 18 months. They are very complex with a lot of due diligence and analysis.

“There are teams of 10-20 people working on a deal for many, many months. This starts with going to clients for early-stage meetings, and when you go to these meetings you have to be prepared. You probably saw a lot of Wall Street movies, and there, you see a lot of analysts working through the paperwork and creating folders. This is an iconic cliche scene, but that preparation can be done with AI today.”

title: Waste-to-energy firm picks Stackable on Ionos for sovereignty
raw_text:
Martin, a Munich-based company that builds waste-to-energy plants, has deployed the open-source Stackable data platform on German cloud provider Ionos – a move it said keeps its plant telemetry beyond the reach of US hyperscalers and the US Cloud Act.

The firm is a fourth-generation family business founded in 1925 by engineer Josef Martin. It designs, builds and services thermal waste treatment plants. It hands each plant to its client – often a municipality or a public-private partnership – and then supports it for years after. Around 250 people work at its Munich headquarters and more than 1,000 across the group, which has built more than 1,100 incineration lines in its century of operation.

Each line carries hundreds of sensors that track combustion, emissions, plant condition and energy recovery. Together they produce about 10GB of telemetry per line each day. Martin previously analysed that data in a decentralised way between different people, tools and manual exports.

“Data sovereignty was very important to us,” said Max Schönsteiner, head of research and development at Martin. “Not because our facilities handle highly sensitive data, but because, as part of our waste management remit, we are part of critical infrastructure and did not want to become dependent on a large hyperscaler.”

That data sovereignty concern drove the choice of Stackable, an open-source, Kubernetes-native big data platform. It packages components such as Apache Spark, Kafka, NiFi, Trino and Superset as Kubernetes operators, so customers assemble only the tools they need and can move the whole data layer between clouds or back on-premises without rebuilding it.

At Martin, the pipeline streams sensor readings from an edge device via MQTT into a NiFi broker, writes them to object storage, then runs Spark jobs scheduled by Airflow into Iceberg tables, queried through Trino and visualised in Superset and Grafana. The only managed service is the Kubernetes cluster itself, supplied by Ionos, and the infrastructure is deployed as code with OpenTofu.

Schönsteiner said the stack is entirely open source, with no licence fees and no proprietary software: “Thanks to Stackable’s open-source capabilities and its universal Kubernetes technology base, we can switch seamlessly to an on-premise solution at any time if we wish.”

What does cloud sovereignty actually mean?

Data sovereignty means keeping control of where data sits and who can reach it, but hosting in the EU is not the same as being beyond US reach. The US Cloud Act lets US authorities compel US companies to hand over data even when it is stored overseas, so the hardware and software inside a “European” cloud matters as much as its jurisdiction.

Martin chose Ionos partly to sidestep that reach, but Schönsteiner admitted the company did not scrutinise what the provider itself runs: “I did not look that deep into the Ionos infrastructure. However, they claim that they are offering full sovereignty.”

That’s where there is a potential gap: a German datacentre does not by itself mean no US equipment or US software sits inside it, and sovereignty ultimately depends on the whole stack, not just the location.

For UK enterprises weighing the same Cloud Act and hyperscaler dependence questions, Martin’s deployment is a working example of what practical cloud sovereignty looks like – an exit option built into the architecture, rather than a promise from a supplier.

That exit option was central to the decision. Ionos – a subsidiary of German telecoms group United Internet, which runs Martin’s compute in Frankfurt – is a German company under European law. Schönsteiner said the US Cloud Act effectively gave US authorities “an entry gate” into data held by US companies, and that he wanted a provider with no US parent.

Martin frames predictive maintenance as the destination but has not yet shipped a machine-learning product. “We are currently working on different AI ideas, but we do not yet have a full product,” Schönsteiner said. 

The near-term work is data quality and curation, then a semantic layer so staff can “talk to the plant data” through a large language model. He said predictive maintenance on core waste processing line components – such as boilers and furnaces – is hard, because availability is the plant’s most important metric and the cost of a wrong call is high.

The immediate gain is harmonisation, he said, adding: “We now combine physical-thermodynamic models with measurement data and further operational information – or, to put it another way: experience meets technology.”

The roll-out began in January 2023 and reached full production within around two years. It is now live across Martin’s sites, with 35 lines connected so far. The company plans to equip as many of its lines as possible, then package the analytics as a service for plant operators.

title: Beyond Nvidia: how alternative silicon is reshaping datacentre design
raw_text:
Nvidia’s approach to artificial intelligence (AI) is raw power in action. Electricity flows into datacentres, and electrons are turned into the tokens that fuel AI workloads. After being processed by the supplier’s ever more powerful graphics processing units (GPUs), the outcome is whatever the outcome a given enterprise or service provider requires.

It is no surprise then that companies’ and countries’ success in the AI battle is measured in the number of MW, or rather GW, of datacentre capacity they’ve deployed. This means ever more power density – and ever more heat.

This has shaped datacentre design over recent years. Demand for power influences the location of facilities, whether that’s repurposed legacy industrial sites with existing grid access, locations in the Nordics with cheap, abundant hydropower, or massive greenfield sites with off-grid power generation. On-site, power kit takes up an increasing share of overall footprint, while liquid cooling is now an essential for AI facilities, but which increases the proportion of non-IT – “grey” – space.

It’s easy to take as truth that Nvidia’s chip roadmap will continue to dictate datacentre design for the next decade, but there are hints that we should expect a more diverse datacentre landscape in the future. 

CPUs out of the GPU shadow

“Accelerated” computing dominates AI spend, and Nvidia dominates the market for accelerated computing. Having said that, IDC noted last February that “x86 and non-x86 systems saw strong adoption as AI platforms scaled infrastructure to meet rising training and inference requirements”.

That rising demand for inference and agentic AI has implications for what goes into datacentres, explains Leo Gergs, research director at ABI Research. That means it plays to Intel, as well as to AMD’s legacy.  

Other players are hoping to grab a slice of the market too. Qualcomm is pushing its own reference designs for AI racks. And Nvidia has its Grace Hopper architecture, which closely couples Arm-based CPU tech with Nvidia’s GPU silicon on a single chip. However, none of these initiatives are really seeing traction yet, Gergs adds.

But according to Dilip Ramachandran, senior director for segment marketing for Arm’s Cloud AI unit, the rise of agentic AI pushes the bottleneck to CPUs in traditional setups where a single CPU is in front of two GPUs.

“So, we are talking to a number of customers who are adding CPU clusters to manage tool calling, the orchestration in particular, but also some aspects of reasoning and planning as well,” he says.

Gergs says ABI Research expects the ratio of CPUs to GPUs in datacentres to be in the region of six to one, or even seven to one. With CPUs drawing a fraction of the power their Nvidia-branded equivalents suck up, that should rewrite the power and cooling equation for datacentre designers. But it’s not just non-accelerated computing that’s being targeted by alternative silicon suppliers.

Alternative acceleration

Broadcom’s focus is on accelerated computing parts tailored to customer software and AI models. They operate in a much tighter energy envelope than Nvidia’s flagship chips, which has implications for the amount of power and cooling kit datacentre operators need to design in. Its customer roster includes hyperscalers such as Google and Meta, as well as model makers OpenAI and Anthropic. 

“Our six XPU customers are accelerating the adoption of custom accelerators, and AI semiconductor revenue more than tripled year over year to $16.7bn,” Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said on its most recent earnings call. “During the quarter, we delivered Ironwood TPU v7 in high volume to both Anthropic and Google.”

Tan claimed the next generation TPU v8i it has begun shipping for Google is optimised for inference workloads, and “in performance, it is comparable – if not surpasses – the Vera Rubin GPU”, adding: “The lesson here is when you co-develop a chip that is optimised for your particular LLM workloads, you will outperform any GPU.” And at substantially lower cost.

Beyond Broadcom, Arm’s Ramachandran points out there are a cohort of alternative accelerator suppliers coming up, many of which Arm is partnering with. They are focused on power efficiency and will likely be targeted at specific tasks. He cites Nvidia’s own deal with Groq to boost the GPU giant’s inference capabilities.

“That’s where you’re going to have a mix of GPUs in the datacentre,” he predicts. “You’re going to have accelerators which are more power efficient.”

Nvidia has advantages which can potentially keep it at the heart of datacentre design, however. Its Cuda platform has underpinned the growth of AI, and effectively ties developers to its platform. But the Cuda moat may become less important, Gergs says, with the gap between AMD’s ROCm and Cuda becoming less significant: “It gradually loses its importance with agentic.”

Power and sovereignty: A shift to the edge?

A few years ago, the search for Nvidia GPU silicon was a government-level concern. Now, it looks like datacentre designers and operators will have a far wider silicon menu to choose from – but that doesn’t mean datacentre operators are ripping up blueprints entirely.

“Alternative silicon still needs the same energy and cooling to deliver comparable results. Dies are getting smaller and more efficient, but they also provide more compute, so the heat and power profile remains the same,” says Richard Collar, vice-president of customer solutions, Kao Data. So, the “backbone infrastructure” stays the same, and from Kao Data’s perspective, “liquid cooling becomes a necessity”.

But other constraints move on a different timescale. Planning approval for datacentres – even when accelerated – is still measured in months and years, as are construction timescales. Grid connections can be measured in decades.

In the meantime, the shift to inference makes edge or metro sites with existing power and comms connections a more attractive option, especially as they are closer to customers.

The focus on sovereignty and data privacy also shapes datacentre placement, says Gergs. Compute will, in some cases, need to be nearer to the data source, to speed inference and to allay sovereignty or privacy concerns. That shift to the edge, Gergs adds, will mean an increased focus on reference designs and modular designs.

Time to breakup?

Meanwhile, specialist inference providers are coming over the horizon.

“You will see datacentres breaking up,” says Gergs. “For a number of reasons, particularly when you look at the inference discussion [where] proximity to the data source becomes somewhat important.”

That’s the rationale behind Vector Core Compute, backed by Vista Equity, which uses SambaNova’s architecture for token generation in combination with Nvidia for pre-fill, and Intel Xeon for inference and orchestration.

SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang describes the objective as a “focus on ultra low latency, ultra low cost by deploying AI in the top 50 metropolitan cities in the United States,” adding that this approach is “very pertinent to the European sovereign story” because the two main limiters are the sizing of power and land.

“I think the enterprises are just waking up,” Liang says. “For you to actually engage with businesses, real-time is going to be important, and real-time means you’ve got to be where people do business.” That means places where power and land is at a premium. “You can’t drop a gigawatt datacentre in the middle of London.”

No government is going to exclude the big hyperscalers from their national AI strategies, Liang says, but governments and customers will want a choice. “It’s going to be heterogeneous,” he says. “Governments are going to bring in a mix, right?”

More importantly, SambaNova has stated that “Vista’s enterprise AI inference cloud, utilises air cooling to deliver sustainable, low-cost inference”,  although it’s not clear whether its sites will be entirely air-cooled.

Arm’s Ramachandran is less convinced about extended life support for air cooling. The demand for AI is so high that datacentre operators will do whatever they can to extract maximum performance from every watt they can get into their facility. And, he says, set against rack costs in the millions, the extra cost of liquid cooling compared to air is marginal.

“Once you have a hall that’s liquid cooled, then you typically have only liquid cooled servers in there,” he says. “So, they expect the CPU to be liquid cooled, and they want it to be dense compute.”

Kao Data’s Collar agrees, adding: “Future data halls will host CPU, GPU and quantum racks side by side, complementing one another. Our job is to deliver high-density power and cooling to the technology suite, with each rack configuration tailored to the customer, whatever silicon they choose.”

What does this mean for enterprises? Datacentre operators and hyperscalers will no doubt do whatever they can to get capacity deployed.

But ultimately, Gergs suggests, enterprise customers will be largely indifferent to these architectural questions, unless they’re looking to build their own infrastructure: “They’re more interested in clearly answering operational questions like data protection, data privacy.”

They will take inference capacity as and where they can, says Gergs, as long as their data is not being used to train someone else’s model. “The rest I think they don’t really care about,” he says.

title: AIforce World Tour: Salesforce promises free Slack access to UK students
raw_text:
Zahra Bahrololoumi, CEO of Salesforce for UK and Ireland, announced at the supplier’s AIforce World Tour London event that it will provide free Slack Enterprise access to British further and higher education students.

The supplier said the initiative is part of a $6bn investment in the country’s economy.

“Young people will define the next decade of UK business, and it’s imperative that students across all disciplines are able to learn to use AI responsibly,” said Bahrololoumi. “By bringing Slack and AI-powered tools like Slackbot directly into further and higher education, we are giving young people hands-on experience with the exact technology and operating system used by organisations across the UK.
